title: The Machine That Talks

post.author: u/ghostwalk_guide_eydis
post.title: I guide a ghost walk at night. At the churchyard, 20 phones spun in silence at once. Our usage page says the story was told 60 times.

blocks.text: I'm Eydis, night guide for a ghost-walk tour company. The ghosts are only stories: old legends told at 6 stops around town. Each visitor's phone runs our app, which tells each stop's story in the visitor's language. Visitors can also type the app a question.
The stories aren't recorded. The app has a language model write each one fresh: a program that writes text one small piece at a time, a word or part of a word. Each piece is called a token.

Asking for a story goes in steps. At a stop I cue it from my phone, and every visitor's phone sends a request: the stop's instructions, its notes and the visitor's language. Everything the model is given like that is called its context. Then the phone waits for the answer.

The model runs on a provider's machines, in a building we never see. The first token comes after about 1.2 seconds, then about 40 tokens a second. Chat apps show an answer word by word: the line stays open, and each piece is passed to the phone the moment it's written. Ours waits for the whole answer and shows it at once: Tuija, who writes our stops, wanted each story to land whole, like a page.

Every request passes through our gateway: one front door between all our phones and the provider. It keeps a line open to each phone while the answer is written. If a line carries nothing for 30 seconds, the gateway closes it. That's its silence limit, set years ago for short replies.

When the gateway closes a line, the app tries again by itself: it sees the line close, sends the same request again at once, and waits, twice at most. Each new try is called a retry. Every stop also has a cap: the most tokens its story may use. Stops were capped at 800 tokens, so a story took 1.2 + 20 = 21.2 seconds.

On Thursday afternoon, 15 October, Tuija changed the instructions for stop 4, the churchyard, to "tell the full legend". That legend runs to 1,400 tokens, so she raised the stop's cap from 800 to 1,400. Her writing tool, which asks the provider directly, not through the gateway, showed the whole legend.
Tonight's walk, the only one, left at 21:00. Stops 1 to 3 went as always. At 22:10 we reached the churchyard and I cued stop 4.
Twenty phones lit up with the same spinning circle, all at once, among the graves.
Nothing came. At 22:11:30 a woman by the gate read hers aloud: "Sorry, the story is taking too long." Every screen said the same.
On my tablet I opened the provider's usage page, which counts the answers it wrote for us, and our app log, which counts what reached a phone. Each line: the stop, stories billed, stories delivered:
Sixty answers for twenty visitors, 84,000 tokens of story, and not one arrived. Our own records show the provider writes each answer to its end even after the gateway hangs up, and counts it.

blocks.label: stop4_one_phone.png

diagram.aria: One visitor's phone at stop 4, Thursday 15 October 2026, from 22:10:00 for 100 seconds. The model is writing from 22:10:00 to 22:11:36.2. Try 1's line is silent from 0 to 30 seconds and cut; try 2's from 30 to 60 and cut; try 3's from 60 to 90 and cut. The phone screen spins from 0 to 90 seconds, then shows the sorry message. Markers: 22:10:30 cut, 22:11:00 cut, 22:11:30 sorry.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the app log, the usage page and my sums, Thursday 15 October 2026, for one of the 20 phones; all 20 did the same. The app tags each request with its stop, which is how the usage page counts per stop. Stop 4's story is 1,400 tokens: 1.2 + 1,400 ÷ 40 = 1.2 + 35 = 36.2 seconds to write. Each try's line was silent, so the gateway closed it at 30 seconds, 6.2 seconds before the answer would have been ready, and the app asked again at once. Three tries, three cuts, then the sorry at 22:11:30. The provider wrote all three answers to the end, the last at 22:11:36.2, and counted each: 20 × 3 = 60 billed, 60 × 1,400 = 84,000 story tokens.

blocks.text: I've walked those graves a hundred nights. Whatever went quiet tonight was somewhere I've never seen. What should we change before tomorrow's walk?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Some sums first. The wait before the first token is called time to first token; the wait until the last one is the total time. What was the total time for stop 4's new story, and for the old 800-token ones? While the model wrote, what did the gateway see on each line, and for how long? Then count: how many requests did the provider get for stop 4, and how many answers reached a phone?

replies.author: u/ghostwalk_guide_eydis
replies.text: 1.2 + 1,400 ÷ 40 = 1.2 + 35 = 36.2 seconds now; the old ones took 1.2 + 20 = 21.2. The gateway saw nothing on the line, because the answer only comes when it's finished. At 30 seconds it closed each line, and the app asked again, twice: 20 visitors × 3 tries = 60 requests, 60 answers written, 0 reached a phone.

comments.author: u/just_raise_it_tsering
comments.text: The gateway's 30-second limit is the bug. Your story needs 36.2 seconds and the gateway gives it 30, so it can never finish. Raise the limit to 120 and the story gets through on the first try, the retries never fire, and Tuija keeps her full legend. One number in one settings file, changed before tomorrow's walk.

comments.author: u/saved_tales_paloma
comments.text: Why ask a machine for the same legend twenty times a night? Our castle tour writes each stop's story once and plays the saved text. Write all six stops once a night, in every language you offer, and the phones show them at once: no waiting at the grave, and nothing to pay at each stop.

replies.author: u/ghostwalk_guide_eydis
replies.text: Visitors' typed questions would still go to the model, though.

reply.prompt: Tomorrow night's walk reaches the churchyard at 22:10 again. What should the company change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Raise the gateway's silence limit from 30 seconds to 120 seconds, so the long story fits.
options.part2: On Friday 16 October we raised the gateway's silence limit to 120 seconds. At 22:10 I cued stop 4 and twenty phones spun among the graves, saying nothing. In the sim the story arrives whole after 36.2 s of silence, under the 120-second limit: 20 answers billed, 20 delivered. It worked, and it felt broken. Thirty-six seconds is a long time to stare at a spinning circle beside a grave at night; by the twentieth second visitors were shaking their phones, and two walked back to the gate. Nothing about the retries changed either: any line that is cut still sends the whole long request again from the start, and the provider writes and counts the whole answer again.
options.senior: Raising a timeout to fit a slow answer treats the number, not the silence. The line is still silent for the whole total time, now 36.2 seconds, and the visitor sees nothing until the end; time to first token is what a person feels, and this leaves it at 36.2. A silence limit also does a job: it frees lines held by phones that have gone, and at 120 seconds the gateway holds those dead lines four times longer. And the retries are untouched: any cut still repeats the full request, and each repeat is written and billed in full.

options.text: Send the story to the phone word by word as it is made, and cap each stop's length.
options.part2: On Friday 16 October the app went word by word: one line stays open, and each piece the model writes goes straight through the gateway to the phone. Tuija rewrote the churchyard legend to fit 800 tokens, every stop is capped at 800 again, and the app now retries only when no words have arrived at all, never a story already under way. In the sim, word by word with the 800-token cap: first words after 1.2 s, in full after 21.2 s, 20 answers billed, 20 delivered, 16,000 story tokens. At 22:10:01.2 the first lines of the legend appeared on twenty screens, and the churchyard went quiet the right way: twenty people reading by phone-light among the graves.
options.senior: Streaming changes what the gateway sees. One connection stays open and each piece is sent as it is made, so the line is never silent for longer than the time to first token, 1.2 seconds, and the 30-second limit never fires, while the visitor reads from the first second instead of waiting for the last. The cap keeps the total time, and the tokens billed, inside a budget someone chose on purpose: 800 tokens is 21.2 seconds and a known price. And a long request is never retried blindly: a repeat costs the whole answer again, so retry only when nothing has started, and find out why before asking twice.

options.text: Write each stop's story once a night in every language, and play the saved text to visitors.
options.part2: From Friday 16 October Tuija's tool wrote all six stops once a night, before the walk, in every language we offer, and the phones showed the saved text. In the sim: the saved story is shown at 22:10:00 on 20 phones at once, 0 live requests, 0 answers billed. It was instant, and the churchyard was perfect. But every visitor that night read exactly the same legend, and by the second week our regulars could recite it with me. And at stop 4 a boy typed "who is buried under the yew?": his question went live to the model through the same gateway, and his phone waited, silent, for the whole answer.
options.senior: Writing the stories ahead of time is honest engineering: it removes the model from the walk's critical moment, costs a few requests a night instead of sixty at a stop, and is instant. But it gives up what the live model was for: stories that vary and answer the visitor, so the next guide hears the same words every night. And it fixes only part of the system: visitors' own questions still go live, through the same gateway, still waiting for the whole answer. It pairs well with streaming; it does not replace it.

options.text: Retry five times instead of twice, so that one of the tries gets through in time.
options.part2: On Friday 16 October we set the app to retry five times. At 22:10 I cued stop 4. In the sim every try is silent for 30.0 s and cut: 20 visitors × 6 tries = 120 answers billed, 0 delivered, 168,000 story tokens, and every phone shows the sorry at 22:13:00. Three minutes of spinning instead of ninety seconds, among the graves, and twice Thursday's bill for nothing.
options.senior: A retry helps only when the next try can turn out differently: a dropped line, a busy moment. Here every try is the same 36.2-second request meeting the same 30-second limit, so every one fails the same way, and each one is written and billed in full. More retries multiply the cost and the wait and fix nothing. Before retrying, ask whether anything has changed since the last try; if not, the retry is only a second bill.

sim.title: Replay stop 4 on 15 October
sim.lede: You're Eydis, replaying Thursday 15 October 2026 from 22:10:00 at stop 4, the churchyard. As given data: 20 visitors, 20 phones, all asking when the guide cues the stop. The model's first token comes after 1.2 seconds, then 40 tokens a second, so a story of N tokens takes 1.2 + N ÷ 40 seconds: 800 tokens 21.2 s, 1,400 tokens 36.2 s. A bigger model, for comparison: first token after 2.0 seconds, then 20 tokens a second. Without word-by-word sending, the app shows nothing until the whole answer has arrived, so the line is silent all that time; with it, each piece goes to the phone as it is made. The gateway closes any line silent for its limit, 30 seconds as built. After a cut the app asks again at once, twice as built. The cap is set per stop; stop 4's was raised from 800 to 1,400 this afternoon. Billing is the company's own finding from its usage page, not a provider claim: the provider writes each answer to its end after the gateway hangs up and counts it in full. Saved stories show text written earlier, with no live request. Step through the tries one at a time, or play stop 4 to the end.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play as built: three tries, each silent for 30.0 s and cut, 60 answers billed, 0 delivered, 84,000 story tokens, and the sorry at 22:11:30. Turn word by word on: first words after 1.2 s, in full after 36.2 s, 20 billed, 20 delivered. Set the story to 800 tokens with word by word off: 21.2 s, under the limit, delivered. Set the silence limit to 120 seconds: delivered, after 36.2 s of silence. Set retries to 5: 120 billed, 0 delivered, sorry at 22:13:00. Turn saved stories on: 0 live requests. Try the bigger model: even 800 tokens take 42.0 s and are cut. Then the fix: word by word, story 800 tokens, cap 800 for every stop.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the churchyard broke. Stop 4's new legend took 1.2 + 35 = 36.2 seconds to write, and the app shows nothing until the end, so every line sat silent past the gateway's 30-second limit and was cut, retried and cut again: 20 visitors × 3 tries = 60 answers billed, 0 delivered, all of it in buildings the guide never sees.

steps.title: Tokens: the unit of length, time and cost.
steps.text: A language model writes one token at a time, a word or part of a word, so tokens measure everything about an answer. Length: stop 4's legend is 1,400 tokens. Time, in two parts: the time to first token (1.2 seconds here), then the writing speed (40 tokens a second), so total time is 1.2 + 1,400 ÷ 40 = 36.2 seconds, and an 800-token story is 21.2. Cost: providers usually bill by tokens, both the context sent in (the stop's instructions, notes and the visitor's language) and the answer written out. A longer prompt makes a slower, dearer request even before a word comes back. A bigger model is not a cure: bigger models often write fewer tokens a second, and in the sim one that starts after 2.0 seconds and writes 20 tokens a second needs 42.0 seconds even for 800 tokens.

steps.title: A request, a gateway cut and a retry, step by step.
steps.text: First the phone sends its request to the gateway, the company's one front door, which passes it to the provider and keeps the line to the phone open. The model reads the context and writes, token by token. As built, the provider holds the answer until the last token, so nothing crosses the line; what can go wrong is that the gateway cannot tell a slow answer from a dead phone. At 30 seconds of silence it closes the line, a rule set for short replies. The app sees the close and sends the same request again at once, from the start; what goes wrong is that the provider is still writing the first answer, to 22:10:36.2, and the company's own usage records show it counts every one in full. Three tries per phone, 60 answers billed, none delivered. Wait Longer showed what retries that all fire together do to a server; here every retry also repeated a request that could never fit inside the limit.

steps.title: Word by word: the line is never silent.
steps.text: Streaming, in steps: the phone asks once and the line stays open; the provider sends each piece as soon as it is made, as server-sent events, the one-way stream met in The Line That Stays Open, where one connection is held open and the server writes into it as things happen; the gateway passes each piece straight on; the phone shows it. The gateway now sees data every fortieth of a second after the first 1.2 seconds, so a 30-second silence limit never fires, and it can stay short, still catching dead phones quickly. The visitor reads from 1.2 seconds instead of waiting 36.2, so the time to first token, not the total time, is what they feel. What can still go wrong: a line can drop midway, and the phone then holds half a story, so the app needs a rule for that rather than a blind restart. Anthropic's streaming API also sends ping events, small messages that keep a quiet stream from looking idle. LATENT covers the model side in a2e07, Words as They Arrive.

steps.title: Rate limits, and why a blind retry costs twice.
steps.text: Providers cap how much each customer may use. A rate limit counts requests per minute, and also tokens per minute, often input and output separately; go over and the provider refuses with an error, usually 429, and may say how long to wait. Tonight's retries tripled both counts: 60 requests and 84,000 story tokens for 20 stories. On a busier night with several walks at once, blind retries like these are what push an account over its limits, and then even good requests fail. So: cap each stop's length, which fixes the time and the price of every story; retry only when no words have arrived, and wait as long as the provider asks; never repeat a long request just because a line closed. LATENT goes deeper: a6e01, One Door to Every Mind (the gateway), a6e03, Asking Twice Costs Twice, a6e05, Seconds Feel Like Hours (latency), and a6e07, Too Many Questions (rate limits). The wrong ideas: a 120-second limit leaves 36.2 seconds of silence at a grave; five retries bill 120 answers and deliver none; saved stories are instant but stop varying, and typed questions still go live.

steps.title: The walk into the provider's building.
steps.text: Everything Eydis could see was fine: the churchyard, the phones, the app doing exactly what it was told. Tuija's tool had even shown her the whole legend, because it asked the provider directly and waited, with no gateway in between. The cause lived in two buildings nobody on the walk had stood in: the gateway's machines, closing silent lines at 30 seconds by a rule set for short replies, and the provider's machines, writing the legend three times over for every visitor and counting each one. After the last visitor had gone, Eydis sat on the lychgate step and opened the usage page again, and this time read it as a visitor's story told twice and lost twice: twenty phones asking, sixty answers written somewhere far away, and not one word carried back across the line.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for tomorrow's walk. The model provider writes stop 4's story under an 800-token cap at 40 tokens a second, and each piece goes to the gateway as it is made; the gateway passes each piece on, so it is never silent and its 30-second limit stays. The 20 phones show words from 1.2 seconds and the whole story at 21.2 seconds. Below: retry only if no words came, and a cap of 800 tokens for every stop.

nodes.label: Retry only if no words came

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tomorrow's walk. The provider writes the churchyard story under an 800-token cap and sends each piece as it is made; the gateway passes each one straight on, so its line is never silent and its 30-second limit can stay. Twenty phones show the first words after 1.2 seconds and the whole story after 21.2: 20 answers billed, 20 delivered. The app retries only when no words have arrived.

fix.title: The fix: send the story word by word, cap every stop, and never retry a long request blindly
fix.text: Switch the app to word by word: the phone asks once, the line stays open, and each piece goes through the gateway to the phone as it is made, so the gateway's 30-second silence limit can stay as it is and still catch dead phones. Put the cap back at 800 tokens for every stop, and have Tuija write the churchyard legend to fit it, so every story takes about 21.2 seconds and costs a known number of tokens; any stop whose cap must rise is checked against the silence limit and the budget first. Change the retry rule: retry only when no words have arrived at all, wait as long as the provider asks, and never resend a story that has already started. Test changes the way visitors use them, through the gateway, not straight to the provider. Watch three numbers per stop: time to first token, total time, and answers billed against answers delivered.

limits: Streaming moves the problem rather than ending it: a line can still drop halfway through a legend, leaving a visitor with half a story, and the app needs a rule for that (show what arrived and offer to continue) rather than a blind restart.

The cap is a budget, not a law of nature. If the company later wants a longer legend, the cap and the silence limit must be checked together, and the usage page watched, or the next change brings the same night back.

Billing for a request cut off mid-answer is this story's rule, the company's own finding from its usage page. The provider pages read for this case do not say how a cut-off request is billed, so check your own provider's records rather than assuming either way.

explain.seniorTake: Put a language model behind your own front door and you inherit its clock: a wait for the first token, then a steady writing speed, both measured in tokens. Every timeout between the user and the model has to be set against that clock, and the safest way to meet it is to stream, so the line is busy from the first second and people read while the model writes. Cap the length of every answer, because length is time and length is money. Count requests and tokens per minute against your provider's limits, and treat every retry of a long request as a second full bill: retry only when nothing has started, and only after waiting as long as the provider asks.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: limits in requests and tokens per minute
realWorld.text: Anthropic's Rate limits page says: "The rate limits for the Messages API are measured in requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (ITPM), and output tokens per minute (OTPM) for each model class." A burst of blind retries counts against all three.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: a 429 error, and how long to wait
realWorld.text: "If you exceed any of the rate limits you will get a 429 error describing which rate limit was exceeded. When the response has a retry-after header, wait that many seconds before retrying." A retry that ignores that wait only fails again.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: output tokens counted as they are made
realWorld.text: "OTPM rate limits are evaluated in real time as output tokens are produced, counting only the actual tokens generated." That is about rate limits, not billing; the page does not say how a request cut off mid-answer is billed, which is why this story treats that as the company's own finding.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: streaming with server-sent events
realWorld.text: The Streaming messages page says: "When creating a Message, you can set "stream": true to incrementally stream the response using server-sent events (SSE)." It adds: "Event streams may also include any number of ping events."

realWorld.title: Anthropic: idle connections and long requests
realWorld.text: The errors page warns: "Some networks may drop idle connections after a variable period of time, which can cause the request to fail or time out without receiving a response from Anthropic." And: "Consider using the streaming Messages API or Message Batches API for long-running requests, especially those over 10 minutes." The churchyard's gateway was one such network, at 30 seconds.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: retries, twice by default
realWorld.text: "The official SDK automatically retries transient failures (such as connection errors, rate limits, and 5xx server errors) with exponential backoff, twice by default, honoring the retry-after header when present." Twice is a common default; it helps when the next try can turn out differently, and not when every try meets the same limit.

asked: How would you put an API in front of a language model?
What is time to first token, and why does it matter?
Why stream, and what does it change for timeouts and retries?
interview.answer: I'd put one gateway in front of the model provider: it holds the provider's keys, checks who is asking, counts requests and tokens per minute against our limits, and sets a timeout on every line. Then I'd do the sums in tokens, because tokens are length, time and cost: time to first token, the wait before anything appears, plus the answer's length divided by the writing speed gives the total time, and the bill counts the tokens sent in as context and the tokens written out. Time to first token matters because it is what a person feels if you stream; without streaming they wait the whole total time, and every timeout in between has to be longer than that. So I stream: one connection stays open, each piece is sent as it is made, the line is never idle for longer than the first wait, and a short timeout can stay short and still catch dead clients. I cap every answer's length so total time and cost have a ceiling. And I never retry a long request blindly: a retry repeats the whole answer and its bill, so I retry only when nothing has started, and wait as long as the provider asks when it refuses with a 429. I'd tell the story of a ghost walk whose churchyard legend took 36.2 seconds to write behind a gateway that closed lines silent for 30: three tries per phone, sixty answers billed, none delivered.

atWork: A gateway timeout set for short replies meeting a long model answer is a common pattern: nothing changes in the gateway, a prompt or a length setting grows, and one day the answers stop arriving while the bill keeps rising. Walk the path from your user to the model and list every timeout on it: the app, any gateway or load balancer, the provider's own client. For each, compare it with the slowest total time your answers can reach, which is time to first token plus the length cap divided by the model's writing speed. If any timeout is shorter, stream the answer, or raise the timeout on purpose and write down why. Make sure every request carries a length cap, chosen with the timeouts and the budget in view, and that a change to it is reviewed like any other change. Check your retry rule: does it resend a long request from the start after a cut, and does it wait as long as a 429 asks? Watch time to first token, total time, and answers billed against answers delivered; when the two counts part, something between you and the provider is throwing work away. Find out from your own usage records how your provider bills a request cut off mid-answer, rather than assuming. Standards: if your company is pursuing the NIST AI Risk Management Framework or ISO/IEC 42001, the AI systems they cover include ones like this, and the timeouts, caps, retry rules and usage monitoring above are the kind of evidence their reviews look for; build them in from the first design rather than at audit time. This case names those frameworks; it does not teach them.

recall.prompt: Your company adds a "summarise this report" button that sends a whole report to a language model through your own gateway. The gateway drops any connection idle for 60 seconds, the app shows the summary only when it is complete, and the app retries twice. Short reports work; long ones fail every time, and the cost of that button is three times what you planned. What is happening, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: A long summary takes longer to write than the gateway allows, and nothing crosses the connection until it is done
Stream the answer so pieces flow as they are written and the connection is never idle for long
Each retry repeats the whole request and is billed again; cap the length and never retry a long request blindly

recall.model: The long summaries take longer to write than the gateway allows, and because the app waits for the whole answer, nothing crosses the connection until it is done: the line looks silent, so at 60 seconds the gateway drops it. The app then retries twice, each try sends the whole request again, and the provider writes and is paid for every one, which is why the cost tripled while nothing arrived. I'd stream the answer, so each piece goes to the user as it is written and the connection is never idle for longer than the time to first token; I'd cap the length of every summary so the total time and cost have a ceiling; and I'd stop blind retries: retry only when nothing has started, and find out why before asking twice.

recall.prompt: In the sim, as built at stop 4 (1,400 tokens, a 30-second silence limit, 2 retries), which one change gets the story to all 20 phones with the first words after 1.2 seconds?
recall.why: Word by word sends each piece as it is made, so the first words reach the phones after 1.2 s and the line is never silent long enough to be cut; the story is in full after 36.2 s, 20 billed, 20 delivered. A 120-second limit delivers too, but only after 36.2 s of silence. Five retries bill 120 and deliver 0. The bigger model makes it worse: 72.0 s for the legend.

recall.prompt: Anthropic's Rate limits page says the Messages API's limits are measured in three ways. Which three?
options: Requests per second, open connections and gigabytes a day
Requests, input tokens and output tokens, each per minute
Words per hour, users and models
Answers per day, characters and pages
recall.why: The page says the limits "are measured in requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (ITPM), and output tokens per minute (OTPM) for each model class". A blind retry counts against all three.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what is time to first token, and why does it matter when you put an API in front of a language model?

keyIdeas.idea: It is the wait before the first piece appears; total time adds the length divided by the writing speed
With streaming it is the wait a person feels; without streaming they wait the whole total time
Every timeout in front of the model must allow for it; streaming keeps the connection busy so short timeouts don't cut answers

recall.model: Time to first token is the wait before the model's first piece appears, before anything is shown. The total time adds the answer's length divided by the writing speed, the tokens a second. It matters because, if you stream, sending each piece as it is made, the first wait is what a person feels; without streaming they wait the whole total time staring at nothing. It also matters for the API in front: every timeout between the user and the model has to allow for it. Without streaming, a connection carries nothing until the end, so any idle timeout shorter than the total time cuts every long answer; with streaming the connection is never silent for longer than the first wait, so a short timeout can stay short and still catch dead clients.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. Word by word has run every night since October, every stop is capped at 800 tokens, and the app retries only when no words have arrived. For the Christmas season the company added walks: on Saturday 12 December, four walks of 20 visitors each left at 21:00, and the guides cued stop 1 in the same minute. Our account may receive at most 50,000 tokens of written answer in any one minute (given data from the provider's limits page). 80 phones asked for an 800-token story at once. 62 got their stories; 18 got an error, "too many requests", each saying to wait 20 seconds. The app asked again at once, since no words had arrived, and those 18 failed again, and again.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did 18 phones fail at stop 1, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The account went over its limit on tokens written per minute: 80 stories of 800 tokens is 64,000, over 50,000, so about 62 fit
Honour the wait the error asks for and back off, instead of retrying at once
Spread the load: stagger the four walks' cues, or ask the provider for a higher limit

coldCase.model: The limit that bit was the one on tokens written per minute, not requests: 80 phones × 800 tokens is 64,000 tokens in one minute, over the account's 50,000, so 62 stories fit (62 × 800 = 49,600) and the other 18 were refused. The retry rule made it worse: no words had arrived, so the app asked again at once, while the minute was still full, and failed again. Each error carried a retry-after of 20 seconds; honour it, and back off with a little jitter so the 18 don't all return in the same instant. Then spread the load: stagger the four walks' cues a minute or two apart, so the stops don't all ask in the same minute, and if the season needs four walks at once, ask the provider for a higher rate limit on output tokens before the next one.
